strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across 8 benchmarks and multiple VLM architectures (3B-72B), demonstrating consistent improvements (51.8-108.8% on MindCube-Tiny)
Novel perspective on enabling intrinsic 3D reasoning in VLMs without requiring external tools at inference time, unlike methods such as Ego3D-VLM
Interpretability advantage through recovery of 3D point clouds from latent representations, providing visual explanations of the reasoning process
Well-designed two-stage training pipeline with clear motivation: supervised alignment (Stage 1) followed by outcome-driven RL refinement (Stage 2)
Thorough ablation studies examining latent size, token position, projector architecture, and reward components
Demonstrates strong generalization across different base VLM architectures and scales without model-specific tuning
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines established techniques (distillation, special tokens, GRPO) without introducing novel algorithmic contributions; individual components are straightforward

Misleading framing regarding external dependencies: the method fundamentally relies on VGGT (3D foundation model) for feature supervision during training, which contradicts the 'no external priors' claim; no analysis of sensitivity to choice of 3D model

Questionable quality of learned 3D representations: visualizations in Fig. 4 show crude, noisy point clouds; no quantitative evaluation metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance, 3D IoU) to validate reconstruction quality or geometric fidelity
Missing critical comparison with most relevant baseline (Mirage [79]), which is acknowledged as 'the most relevant mental model' but not directly evaluated in main results

Severe hyperparameter sensitivity demonstrated in Table 5: latent size of 12 is optimal; using 16 or 32 causes catastrophic performance drops (25.1% and 15.5% respectively), raising generalization concerns

Data construction concerns: only 10K training examples from MindCube; data generated via GPT-4o (proprietary model) with unexplained prompting strategy; no analysis of data quality or diversity impact
No computational cost analysis: training time, inference overhead, and memory requirements not reported; Stage 1 + Stage 2 cost compared to baselines unknown
Marginal improvements on certain sub-tasks (e.g., Travel Time in Ego3D-Bench shows minimal gains), and limited failure case analysis to understand failure modes

Evaluation scope limited to spatial reasoning tasks; unclear whether 3D thinking helps or harms performance on other VLM benchmarks; all benchmarks share similar characteristics (limited-view reasoning)

Contradictions in technical descriptions: limitations section states 3D latents are 'not autoregressively incorporated,' contradicting earlier framework descriptions; projector is frozen in Stage 2 without justification for why joint optimization was not attempted

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations of text-only spatial reasoning in VLMs, with compelling connection to human 3D cognitive abilities
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8+ diverse benchmarks with consistent improvements over strong baselines including recent VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-OneVision)
Thoughtful two-stage training framework that elegantly combines supervised learning with outcome-based reinforcement learning, reducing dependence on dense annotations
Extensive ablation studies (Tables 3-6, 11) systematically validating design choices for latent size, token positioning, projector configuration, and loss components
Interpretable approach with visualizations of reconstructed 3D point clouds that provide transparency into learned representations during reasoning
Practical data generation strategy creating synthetic CoT data from MindCube without requiring additional manual annotation
Clear presentation with effective framework visualization (Figure 2) and logical paper organization
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - primarily an engineering combination of existing techniques (VLMs, standard 3D foundation models, conventional reward formulations) with no novel algorithmic contributions

Insufficient evidence that true 3D spatial reasoning is learned rather than pattern memorization: simple alignment loss (Eq. 5), noisy point cloud visualizations, and lack of rigorous analysis of learned representations
Evaluation scope narrowly confined to MindCube-derived spatial QA tasks without real-world spatial reasoning tasks, limiting claims about generalization beyond benchmark-specific improvements

Heavy dependence on synthetic data from MindCube and specific VGGT features raises reproducibility and generalization concerns; data generation via GPT-4.1 lacks detail on success rates and quality validation

Missing critical analyses: no statistical significance testing, no inference time/memory overhead comparison, no ablation isolating Stage 2's contribution, and modest improvements in some cases (88.9% vs. 83.2%)
Stage 2 (reinforcement learning) contribution unclear - Table 11 ablation doesn't isolate Stage 2's value, and many improvements appear achievable with Stage 1 alone
Limited failure analysis with only one case shown; no systematic characterization of failure modes or guidance for addressing identified limitations
Unclear if improvements stem from 3D reasoning or increased model capacity from adding 3D tokens - no comparison with equivalent capacity baseline without 3D components
High computational cost (21.84h + 12.85h on H100) and complex two-stage training with multiple hyperparameter sets (6 configurations mentioned) limit practical adoption without efficiency analysis
No cross-dataset generalization experiments, evaluation on real images, or justification of why VGGT features are optimal for 3D reasoning
